title: Housing provider funding changes and earlier paramedic dispatch system
subtitle: Also covered: drug strategy update, Indigenous-led child development program, interim housing plan, and a Cambridge women and youth shelter.
overview: The Community and Health Services Committee dealt mainly with two recommendations. The first responds to new provincial regulations under the Housing Services Act. As mortgages end for community housing providers, the committee recommended a new funding model, an annual reinvestment plan, and a new asset limit policy for rent-geared-to-income households {{vote:m1}}. This affects about 27 non-profit and co-op housing providers and roughly 3,200 deeply affordable units.

The second recommendation asks the Ministry of Health to bring the Medical Priority Dispatch System to the Cambridge ambulance dispatch centre as soon as possible {{vote:m2}}. Staff said the current system sends most calls out as lights-and-sirens responses and cannot reassign crews to sicker patients. Staff also said the province fully funds the dispatch centre, so the change would carry no cost to the Region.

The committee also received reports on a new Indigenous-led child development program with SOAHAC and on the Waterloo Region Integrated Drug Strategy. It heard a verbal interim housing update, which gave April 15, 2023 as the target move-in date for the Erb St. shelter. It directed staff to advocate for inhalation services at consumption and treatment sites, to update drug use statistics, and to report on steps toward a Cambridge women and youth shelter. These are recommendations that Council will consider later.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff draft a funding model for community housing providers at end of mortgage, develop an annual reinvestment plan, and let providers keep operating surpluses within set limits.

decisions.item: Asset limit policy for rent-geared-to-income households
decisions.detail: The committee recommended endorsing a new Asset Limit Policy with limits of $75,000 for single households and $100,000 for larger households receiving rent-geared-to-income subsidy.

decisions.item: Service and exit agreements with housing providers
decisions.detail: The committee recommended authorizing the Commissioner of Community Services to enter into service or exit agreements as providers reach end of mortgage, in a form satisfactory to the Regional Solicitor.
The committee recommended that the Region request the Ministry of Health adopt the Medical Priority Dispatch System at the Cambridge Central Ambulance Communications Centre as soon as possible.

The committee recommended directing paramedic leadership to keep working with the Ministry and neighbouring services, and the Chair, Council, CAO, Commissioner and Medical Officer of Health to lobby provincial officials.

debate: On housing, the transcript shows little debate. Staff described the changes as the biggest for the not-for-profit and co-op housing sector in over 20 years, and one councillor welcomed letting providers build reserves.

On the drug strategy, a councillor argued that the consumption site sees only a small share of people who use drugs, and asked how to reach people using at home or smoking substances. Delegates said inhalation services and longer hours are the main gaps, and that provincial funding rules block inhalation services.
Delegates named pilot-style funding, turned-away clients and limited staff supports as barriers. They said advocacy to federal and provincial governments is the strongest tool municipalities have.

Some councillors asked about the drug strategy's lack of current targets and an implementation plan, and about its outdated website and its role relative to public health. Strategy representatives said it had just moved to a project-based model, was updating its materials, and was still setting priorities on stigma and housing.

On dispatch, staff said the current system sends lights-and-sirens responses to about 80% of calls, which stops crews being reassigned to sicker patients and affects rest periods and overtime. One councillor asked for a dollar figure in the motion, and staff answered that the province fully funds the dispatch centre. Councillors reworded the motion's opening to stress call volume and lack of paramedic resources.
